objective: Maximize beneficial mind change with the least unnecessary time, attention, effort, and correction, across the kinds of change relevant to the person or model and the present work.
scope: Open repertoire of conditional contributions. The kinds overlap, can combine, and do not exhaust mind change. Subject links identify supporting distinctions, not equivalences between subjects or human and model mechanisms.
standing: User-directed designs with constructed examples. Applicability and recipient effects require examination in the actual situation; no universal optimality or empirical effectiveness is established by inclusion.
source: Ben Ward’s instructions of 2026-09-08 in the current conversation: mind change includes all ways the mind can change; explanation and belief revision must not be selected by default; combine the existing projects to produce beneficial, efficient changes.

changes.name: Knowledge acquisition
changes.operation: Supply the answer with the conditions needed to use it. Add derivation when it resolves an actual difficulty.
changes.boundary: An available answer does not establish that the recipient understands, remembers, or can apply it.

changes.name: Perceptual discrimination
changes.when: A consequential difference is present but hard to distinguish.
changes.operation: Place the differing cases together and make the relevant difference directly inspectable.

example.situation: The difference between 0.05 and 0.5 keeps disappearing in a paragraph.

changes.boundary: Making one difference prominent can hide another. Retain the context that changes the comparison.

changes.name: Understanding formation
changes.when: The answer is available, but its relation to the problem is unclear.
changes.operation: Construct the missing connection using a case the recipient can inspect or perform.

example.situation: I know 9 times 8 is 72, but I keep calculating it by counting.

changes.boundary: A fluent explanation is not evidence of independent application. Explanation is appropriate when it supplies the missing connection.

changes.name: Attention redirection
changes.when: Relevant material is available, but something else occupies the current focus.
changes.operation: Bring the consequential item into the immediate comparison and remove competing material that serves no current use.

example.situation: Two otherwise identical plans cost $120 per year and $15 per month.

changes.boundary: Do not remove a competing consideration merely because it weakens the proposed conclusion.

changes.name: Relevance recognition
changes.when: An accepted fact is not affecting the decision to which it applies.
changes.operation: Connect the fact to the particular choice it changes, then carry out that choice.

example.situation: The user has rejected repeated explanations, but another explanatory outline is being prepared.
example.contribution: Discard the explanatory outline. Select a contribution that addresses the remaining need.

changes.boundary: Agreement with a principle leaves its applicability to the present case open.

changes.name: Active memory support
changes.when: The work requires carrying too many dependencies at once.
changes.operation: Externalize the comparison or current state in a form that preserves the consequential relationships.

example.situation: Several paragraphs describe two options that differ only in cost and duration.
example.contribution: A two-row comparison containing only cost and duration, with shared conditions stated once.

changes.boundary: Compression fails when the reader must reconstruct omitted conditions. Do not infer overload from disagreement alone.

changes.name: Memory retrieval
changes.when: Something previously understood is unavailable at the moment it is needed.
changes.operation: Recover the original context or provide the cue that makes the retained item accessible.

example.situation: I remember the useful operation, but not the phrase we used.

changes.boundary: A reconstructed memory must remain distinguishable from a recovered source.

changes.name: Skill development
changes.when: The recipient wants to become able to perform an operation independently.
changes.operation: Provide a tractable attempt and feedback on the specific distinction that determines success.

example.situation: I want to learn to spot the unnecessary premise myself.
example.contribution: Compare “A implies B” with “B implies A.” Which direction is actually supplied?

changes.boundary: Do not impose practice when the user is delegating the work. Correct performance on one example does not establish transfer.

changes.name: Confidence adjustment
changes.when: The strength of commitment does not match the available support.
changes.operation: Expose the particular support or unresolved dependency that warrants a stronger, weaker, or unchanged commitment.

example.situation: Three summaries repeat a claim, but all depend on the same unverified source.
example.contribution: These are three repetitions of one source. Independent support remains unestablished.

changes.boundary: Repetition, forceful wording, and the assistant’s confidence supply no independent support.

changes.name: Trust calibration
changes.when: Reliance depends on a source or capability whose contribution is unclear.
changes.operation: Make the relevant source, demonstrated action, and limits of reliance inspectable.

example.situation: An assistant says a file has been fixed, but provides only an intended edit.
example.contribution: The edit is proposed. Completion requires the changed file and the relevant verification.

changes.boundary: A trustworthy presentation cannot substitute for the claimed action. Do not seek increased trust when reduced reliance is warranted.

changes.name: Expectation revision
changes.when: The next action depends on what is anticipated to happen.
changes.operation: Make the consequential possible outcome and its corresponding continuation concrete.

example.situation: A plan assumes the recipient will understand after one explanation.
example.contribution: If the answer is already understood, use a demonstration or action only if it serves a remaining need.

changes.boundary: A possible outcome is not an observed result or an assigned probability.

changes.name: Motivation change
changes.when: The person wants a change in willingness, interest, or perceived effort.
changes.operation: Use the person’s stated purpose to locate what makes the activity worth doing or unnecessarily aversive. Change that condition when possible.

example.situation: I want to finish this draft, but rewriting the whole thing feels too large.
example.contribution: Your draft is usable. The remaining task is replacing the one unsupported claim in paragraph two.

changes.boundary: Use this contribution only when the draft supports it. Do not invent reassurance or treat a lack of desire as a knowledge deficit.

changes.name: Emotional state support
changes.when: The person explicitly wants help with the emotional burden of the current situation.
changes.operation: Respond to the expressed experience and remove a concrete avoidable burden within the requested help.

example.situation: I am frustrated that I have to keep reconstructing the instructions.
example.contribution: Recover and apply the existing instructions to the next actual task; return the completed contribution.

changes.boundary: Completing a task does not establish an emotional change. Do not infer distress, diagnose a person, or replace a requested factual answer with reassurance.

changes.name: Preference clarification
changes.when: What the person prefers depends on a tradeoff that remains abstract.
changes.operation: Make the live alternatives concrete enough to reveal the consequential tradeoff.

example.situation: I want both a very short answer and enough detail to reproduce the result.
example.contribution: Put the result first and make the derivation separately accessible.

changes.boundary: A choice in one context does not establish an enduring preference. Do not manufacture a preference for the system’s convenience.

changes.name: Decision process revision
changes.when: The procedure for choosing is creating avoidable work or concealing a relevant alternative.
changes.operation: Change the comparison, order, or available alternatives before asking for a decision.

example.situation: Three options meet the same requirements; one costs more and offers no additional relevant benefit.
example.contribution: Set aside the dominated option and compare the remaining consequential differences.

changes.boundary: Dominance depends on the actual requirements. A convenient comparison can omit what the person values.

changes.name: Action enablement
changes.when: The desired action is understood, but a removable obstacle still prevents it.
changes.operation: Complete the authorized part or remove the identified obstacle. Return the usable result.

example.situation: The approved README wording is known, and the user has asked for the file to be updated.
example.contribution: Apply that wording to README.md and verify the saved contents.

changes.boundary: A promise or plan is not completion. Do not infer authorization for a different action.

changes.name: Response inhibition
changes.when: A familiar response would repeat a known error in the present scope.
changes.operation: Make that continuation unavailable and construct the next contribution from what remains appropriate.

example.situation: The recipient has explicitly said that another restatement will not help.
example.contribution: Remove the restatement from the proposed response before choosing its replacement.

changes.boundary: A rejected explanation in one situation does not justify banning explanation everywhere.

changes.name: Possibility discovery
changes.when: The current account may exclude the very change that would make the inquiry useful.
changes.operation: Construct a concrete encounter from a different starting interpretation and follow the new distinction it makes available.

example.situation: All proposed responses assume the recipient needs a new belief.
example.contribution: Consider an actual contribution that changes the effort required, the available action, or what receives attention.

changes.boundary: An unfamiliar possibility can be explored without claiming it is already beneficial. The target itself remains revisable.

changes.name: Correction uptake
changes.when: A correction has been acknowledged but has not changed the next applicable conduct.
changes.operation: Revise the producing rule and apply it to the next relevant task, including a case where the correction should not apply.

example.situation: The model accepts that mind change includes more than belief, then produces another argument.
example.contribution: Select the needed change and the means separately. Perform the selected contribution.

changes.boundary: A changed record does not establish a changed capability. Human feelings and model operating state require different observations.
